title: Infrastructure as Code Guide: How to Choose the Right Developer Tools Platform
description: Practical infrastructure as code guidance with planning steps, controls, failure tests, and a readiness checklist.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Choose what should be managed as code
sections.body: Inventory infrastructure that needs repeatable creation, review, and recovery: networks, compute, storage, identity policies, monitoring, and deployment configuration. Decide which resources must be controlled through code and which are intentionally managed manually. Start with a bounded environment and document the current state before importing existing resources. Avoid generating code that merely reproduces accidental configuration without review.

sections.title: Define state and ownership
sections.body: Determine where state is stored, who can read or change it, how locking works, and how backups are restored. Treat state files as sensitive because they can contain resource details or secrets. Test concurrent changes, interrupted operations, and recovery from a corrupted or missing state. Keep separate state boundaries for environments or teams where access and blast radius differ.

sections.title: Review modules and reusable patterns
sections.body: Create modules around stable infrastructure patterns with explicit inputs, outputs, versions, and ownership. Avoid over-generalizing a module before multiple real use cases are understood. Document defaults and destructive changes. Test modules against the provider versions and resource types they support, and provide an upgrade path when an input or resource behavior changes.

sections.title: Build a safe change workflow
sections.body: Run formatting, validation, policy checks, and a plan review before applying changes. Protect production credentials and require approval for destructive operations. Ensure the plan corresponds to the commit that will be applied and that no one can silently change configuration between review and deployment. Make rollback expectations explicit; infrastructure changes often need a forward fix rather than a simple reversal.

sections.title: Manage secrets and least privilege
sections.body: Keep secrets out of code, plans, logs, and pull-request artifacts. Use managed secret storage and short-lived credentials where possible. Scope automation identities to the resources they manage and separate production from non-production access. Test rotation and revocation, and review who can approve changes to IAM policies, network exposure, and public storage.

sections.title: Detect drift and test recovery
sections.body: Schedule drift detection and define how a real difference between code and deployed infrastructure is resolved. Avoid automatically overwriting manual emergency changes before an incident is understood. Test a restore or recreation of a representative resource from code and state. Record which dependencies, data, or secrets cannot be recreated automatically and need a separate recovery plan.

sections.title: Control cost and policy
sections.body: Use policy checks for required tags, encryption, allowed regions, public exposure, and resource types where appropriate. Review cost estimates and quotas before applying large changes. Define who owns policy exceptions and when they expire. Measure failed plans, drift, change lead time, and recovery effort rather than counting the number of resources managed as code.

sections.title: Production readiness checklist
sections.body: Proceed when state is protected, changes are reviewed, secrets are managed safely, destructive actions require appropriate approval, drift is monitored, and recovery has been tested. Document module ownership and provider upgrade practices. Reassess the design as the infrastructure estate or compliance requirements grow.
